newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Albright in Russia for NATO, arms control talks.
newsitem.headline: Albright in Russia for NATO, arms control talks.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright arrived in St Petersburg on Saturday for talks with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov.

The pair, who have developed a considerable personal rapport despite their months of sometimes outspoken duelling over NATO expansion, are expected to try to put their differences behind them and seek progress on a number of arms control issues.

Primakov was on hand to meet Albright when she flew into St Petersburg's Pulkovo airport from Slovenia. They greeted each other with a handshake and kiss before being whisked off to the city. They made no statements to reporters.

Diplomats say Albright will brief Primakov on this week's NATO summit in Madrid, where the formal decision to expand eastward was taken -- a move Primakov on Tuesday called "the biggest mistake in Europe since the end of World War Two".
It was not clear whether Russian objections to a NATO swoop on suspected war criminals in Bosnia, which Russia denounced on Friday as "cowboy raids", would be raised in St Petersburg.

But Albright will discuss arms control during a 19-hour overnight stay in the former tsarist capital and attempt to build on improving ties with Russia following the signing of the NATO-Russia Founding Act in May.

Albright's visit, sandwiched between talks in would-be NATO members Slovenia and Lithuania, comes in a round of whistle-stop European tours by U.S. leaders including President Bill Clinton, following the Madrid summit where former Soviet allies Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic were invited to join.

It also opens a round of diplomatic house calls on Russia by Western foreign ministers. British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook will be in Moscow on Monday and Tuesday. Germany's Klaus Kinkel will discuss NATO with Primakov on Tuesday in the capital.

All are expected to stress a willingness to improve ties with Russia and develop Moscow's cooperation with NATO under the Founding Act, which sought to answer Russian fears over NATO expansion by giving it a say in the alliance's affairs and offering assurances on deployment of NATO forces.
Russian officials, too, have pledged to enhance cooperation and not to dwell on their differences.
U.S. officials say Albright and Primakov will discuss 30-nation negotiations on updating a 1990 treaty limiting conventional arms in Europe and where they are deployed.
They are also expected to discuss the START 2 nuclear arms pact between Moscow and Washington cutting strategic warheads.
Answering a call Russia had made for years, the signatories agreed in December to review the Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty to take account of the split of the Soviet Union.
Sluggish talks in Vienna have been given a new lease of life by the deal signed by Russia and NATO and diplomats have said a new treaty could be ready early next year.
U.S. officials have held out the prospect of even more drastic cuts in nuclear forces -- a START 3 -- if the Russian parliament finally ratifies START 2, signed in 1993.

President Boris Yeltsin told Clinton in April he was confident the communist-dominated State Duma would ratify it. But the nationalist-minded lower chamber, indignant over NATO expansion, seems in no mood to comply.
Yeltsin's spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said on Saturday ratification would be one of Russia's toughest foreign policy issues in months to come.

Primakov and Albright will talk over dinner at a restaurant on Saturday evening and tour the Hermitage art gallery in the tsars' Winter Palace, focus of the 1917 Bolshevik coup d'etat. On Sunday, they will talk over coffee at Albright's hotel.
